Sixth Commandment
SIKSTH kuh-MAND-muhnt
noun (the Decalogue)
From the sixth word of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:13; commandment from Latin mandare, to charge.

Biblical Definition

The Sixth Commandment is the word of the Decalogue that guards human life: "Thou shalt not kill" (Exod 20:13) — more exactly, thou shalt not murder, the unlawful taking of innocent human life. Its ground is the image of God in man: "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man" (Gen 9:6). Because every human being bears the divine image, his life is sacred, and to murder him is an assault upon his Maker. The commandment does not forbid all taking of life — it does not forbid the magistrate's lawful execution of the murderer (the same God who said "thou shalt not kill" commanded capital justice in Gen 9:6 and Rom 13:4), nor lawful war, nor the killing of beasts for food. It forbids murder and the heart from which murder springs. For our Lord drives the commandment inward: whosoever is angry with his brother without cause, and whosoever hates his brother, is a murderer in the heart (Matt 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). Positively, it requires all lawful endeavors to preserve life — our own and our neighbor's. This dictionary confesses the Sixth Commandment as binding moral law, the great wall the law of God sets around the sanctity of human life from the womb to the grave.

Webster 1828 Definition

The word of the Decalogue guarding human life (Exod 20:13): "Thou shalt not kill" — thou shalt not murder. Grounded in the image of God in man (Gen 9:6), it forbids the unlawful taking of innocent life and the hatred from which it springs (Matt 5:21–22), and requires the preserving of life.

SIXTH COMMANDMENT, noun. The sixth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:13), guarding human life.

"Thou shalt not kill" — more exactly, thou shalt not murder, the unlawful taking of innocent life.

Grounded in the image of God in man (Gen 9:6); to murder is to assault the Maker's image.

Does not forbid lawful execution of the murderer, lawful war, or the killing of beasts.

Driven inward by Christ: unjust anger and hatred are murder of the heart (Matt 5:21–22).

Key Scripture

Exod 20:13 — "Thou shalt not kill."

Gen 9:6 — "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."

Matt 5:22 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment."

1 John 3:15 — "Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him."

Modern Corruption

The age cheapens the Sixth Commandment from both ends: it shrinks the sanctity of life so that the unborn, the aged, and the inconvenient may be killed under softening names, and it widens "thou shalt not kill" into a pacifism that forbids the magistrate his God-given sword and the murderer his just penalty.

expand to see more

The gravest corruption of the Sixth Commandment in our day is the assault on innocent life under gentle names — the unborn child destroyed and called a choice, the aged and suffering killed and called mercy. But the commandment guards the image of God in man (Gen 9:6), and that image is borne by the smallest hidden child in the womb. To take that life is murder, however the age relabels it. The dictionary names abortion and euthanasia as violations of this commandment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text, but the words are also stretched the wrong way. Some read "thou shalt not kill" to forbid all taking of life — the magistrate's execution of the murderer, the soldier's lawful war. But the same God who forbade murder commanded capital justice (Gen 9:6) and armed the magistrate with the sword (Rom 13:4). The principle to recover is precise: the commandment forbids murder — the unlawful taking of innocent life — and the hatred behind it (1 John 3:15), and requires every lawful means of preserving life, from the womb to the grave.

Hebrew Roots

From the sixth word of the Decalogue (Exod 20:13); the commandment forbidding murder and the hatred behind it, grounded in the image of God in man (Gen 9:6).
